statement: Set the weekly distance target from the goal-time band, not a fixed template. Faster goals get more weekly km, more runs and longer long runs. Use the 45 km/wk (SD 26) population mean only as a reference point for the display.
value: scaled to goal time; population reference 45.1 km/wk (SD 26.4); fastest group (120-150 min) >3x slower groups
appliesTo: Recreational marathon and half-marathon runners with a time goal

statement: For a competitive marathon goal, plan average build-block volume at or above 40 km/wk where the athlete can safely get there. Below 40 km/wk was associated with slower finishes. Treat as a floor on the target, not a cap. Do not make it a hard requirement for finish-only goals.
appliesTo: Recreational marathoners with a time goal

statement: For a half-marathon time goal, aim for weekly volume above 32 km and a longest run above 21 km before the race; both were associated with faster finishes and less pace decline.
appliesTo: Recreational half-marathon runners with a time goal

statement: Include at least one long run of 25 km or more in the marathon block (a longest run under 25 km was associated with slower finishes). Doherty found more runs of 32 km or more associated with faster cohorts, but gives no count in the abstract. Default as a D-grade value: peak long run 28-32 km, 1-3 such runs, only for athletes already at roughly 50 km/wk or more.
appliesTo: Recreational marathoners

statement: Keep typical session length at about 10 km or more and a longest run of at least 21 km before using weekly volume as the main progression lever. Volume's link to marathon time was significant only above those session lengths. Do not add extra weekly runs as a way to raise performance at fixed volume.
appliesTo: Male-dominated recreational marathon samples; apply to half-marathon and longer as a default, not to 5-10 km goals

statement: Add volume as easy continuous running and keep tempo and interval work as a modest, roughly fixed share. Time in Z2+Z3 was roughly constant across performance levels while Z1 rose with speed. Long-interval work was weakly related to performance in elite men.
value: added km at Z1 (easy); Z2+Z3 share held roughly constant in absolute time
appliesTo: Recreational runners; elite evidence for interval claims only

statement: Default to a pyramidal intensity distribution (most time easy, less at threshold, least above). Set the Z1/Z2 boundary at 82.3% of the athlete's critical speed and the Z2/Z3 boundary at critical speed, estimated from logged runs.
appliesTo: Recreational to fast marathoners with enough logged runs to estimate critical speed

statement: Flag any run of 7 or more consecutive zero-run days in the 16 weeks before a race as a strong negative signal (about 5-8% slower finish in the same runners). Gaps of 6 days or less are common (over half of runners) and not penalised. Schedule so the athlete never goes 7 days without running, especially in the final weeks.
appliesTo: Recreational marathoners

statement: After a 7+ day gap, widen and slow the goal-time projection by about 5-8% (observed cost; larger for faster runners at 5.4% vs 2.6% and late gaps at 5.2% vs 4.4%) and re-plan with a graded restart. The restart fraction is not evidenced: default (grade D) is to resume at about 50-70% of pre-gap weekly volume and rebuild over 2-3 weeks, adjusting to athlete feedback. Engine-rules J7 supersedes the fraction with layoff tiers.
appliesTo: Recreational marathoners who miss 7 or more days in the 16-week window

statement: Show, but do not gate on, the ratio of last-7-day to 28-day load (G-5). Each day at a distance ratio of 1.5 or more was associated with injury (OR 1.06), and a duration-based ACWR was associated with injury (adjusted HR 1.33) only while runners injured at baseline were included. A 1.3 early-warning display is a default (grade D). Combine with athlete-reported soreness or fatigue; never treat the ratio as proof of safe load or as a cap on long-run length.
appliesTo: Recreational 10 km to marathon training

statement: Do not present lower volume as an injury-prevention strategy or higher volume as injury-safe. A review of 36 prospective studies found the evidence on weekly distance, duration, frequency, intensity and their changes conflicting; in short-distance runners lower volume and no running experience were associated with more injury, not less. Keep injury handling adaptive (G-1 spike guard, ramp, feedback, re-plan), not a volume cap.
appliesTo: All recreational runners

statement: For 100 km and longer, do not hard-code whether volume or pace dominates. Use weekly distance, training speed and a recent marathon or half time together, widen the prediction interval, and flag the result as low-evidence. No source here covers 100-mile training volume. Default progression is gradual weekly distance growth (grade D).
value: weekly km + training speed + recent marathon/half time; interval widened
appliesTo: 100 km to 24 h and beyond (including 100-mile) goals

statement: Report the goal or predicted finish time as an interval from at least two sources (a recent race or time trial and a training-based estimate). Do not extrapolate shorter-race times to the marathon with the plain Riegel exponent: it was at least 10 min too fast for half of runners. Include weekly mileage, sex, age, BMI, course gradient and expected weather as inputs.
appliesTo: All race-time and goal-time predictions, marathon especially

statement: Fit a two-parameter performance model (aerobic power index plus endurance decay) to logged duration and distance and re-fit on a rolling window of recent activities so targets follow current fitness. The window length is not given in the abstract; default 8-12 weeks (grade D). Validate against actual race results before relying on it.
appliesTo: Athletes with enough logged duration and distance data

statement: For 5 km and 10 km goals, progress weekly running time first and let run days rise with volume (F5); lengthen the long run only as its share of the growing week. Weekly distance (r = -0.605) and training days (r = -0.583) were the strongest correlates of 10 km time; the longest run was not examined, and no study shows that a longer long run improves 5-10 km performance independently of volume. Do not add run days at a fixed volume as a separate lever (F2).
appliesTo: 5 km and 10 km goals, all volumes

statement: For non-ultra goals the long run is about 0.35 of the week's running time. Coach conventions range from 30% of weekly distance (Daniels, as reported by Running Magazine, under 64 km/week) to about 35-47% implied by an intermediate 5K plan; measured in time, an easy long run is a slightly larger share than in distance, so 0.35 sits inside the range. Convention, labelled as a default.
appliesTo: All non-ultra goals; the tier cap and G-1 bound it

statement: Cap the long run for 5 km and 10 km goals by a volume tier chosen from the runner's completed typical week (median of the last 4 weeks with a run), never from the planned week: 5 km 60 / 75 / 90 min and 10 km 75 / 90 / 100 min at under 180, 180-360 and over 360 min/week. G-1 and G-2 still bind every week, so the cap is reached only from the runner's own history. No minimum long run applies to 5-10 km goals; Johnson's minimums (5 mi for 5K, 7-8 mi for 10K) are context, not floors. The values follow established plans and coaches; they are not evidence-derived.
appliesTo: 5 km and 10 km goals; tier from completed typical weekly running time

statement: For 5 km and 10 km goals the long run is also capped at 16 km (10 miles), the coach and plan maximum for both distances; this binds for faster runners, whose minute cap would otherwise cover more distance. Where Higdon's 90 min advanced 5K long run exceeds 16 km for a fast runner, the more conservative bound wins.
appliesTo: 5 km and 10 km goals, all tiers

statement: No study identifies a safe or unsafe single-session duration; reviews of prospective studies find the evidence on distance, duration and their changes conflicting or low quality. G-1 (each run against the 30-day longest completed run) is the single-session guard. Fixed long-run caps are design defaults and must never be presented as injury limits.
appliesTo: All goals; copy and rule documentation

statement: For new runners (novice experience, or no recent continuous run as long as the floor session), start from a structured, graded programme like Couch to 5K (the E6 start paths), and grow the longest run from the longest recent continuous run under G-1 (0.5 km minimum step) rather than from a share target; during the ladder there is no separate long run. A structured programme was associated with fewer first-year injuries than a self-devised one in a cross-sectional survey, and no running experience is a risk factor; a graded 10%-rule programme did not reduce injuries in an RCT, so no protection is claimed. A published novice 5K plan reaches a longest run of 3 mi (about 30-35 min) after 8 weeks.
appliesTo: Novices and runners in their first year
